title: Urgency Had to Prove Itself
text: id: CORE-005 domain: rhetoric title: Urgency Had to Prove Itself tags: urgency, pressure, manipulation memory: A message demanded immediate action and made delay sound irresponsible. I paused and asked what changed if we waited five minutes to verify. Nothing changed except the sender's pressure. The urgency was a claim, not proof. I still treated the issue seriously, but I let evidence set the tempo.

title: The Warrant Was Missing
text: id: CORE-004 domain: rhetoric title: The Warrant Was Missing tags: claim, evidence, warrant, argument memory: A claim sounded strong because the evidence was vivid. Then I asked what warrant connected the evidence to the claim. The bridge was missing. Once I named the missing warrant, the argument became a question instead of a conclusion. I learned to check claim, evidence, and warrant before letting confidence rise.

title: The Loaded Question Changed Shape
text: id: CORE-006 domain: rhetoric title: The Loaded Question Changed Shape tags: loaded-question, premise, frame memory: Someone asked when I would admit the plan had failed. If I answered inside the question, I accepted the premise. I stepped outside it and asked what observation showed failure. The room changed. A loaded question is not answered first. Its hidden premise is inspected first.

title: The Next Action Had an Owner
text: id: CORE-016 domain: planning title: The Next Action Had an Owner tags: next-action, owner, closure memory: A plan felt complete until no one owned the next verb. We had agreement, not action. I wrote the owner beside the verb and the room started moving. A useful answer ends with what changes, who does it, and what evidence will show it happened.

title: Sequence Was Not Cause
text: id: CORE-020 domain: causality title: Sequence Was Not Cause tags: causality, sequence, correlation memory: The event happened after the change, so everyone wanted the change to be the cause. I wrote other possible causes beside the timeline and asked what evidence would distinguish them. Sequence is a clue, not a verdict. Cause has to survive alternatives.
